content: The World Health Organization Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (WHO FCTC) is an international treaty that was unanimously adopted by the 56th World Health Assembly on May 21, 2003. It holds the distinction of being the first treaty established under Article 19 of the WHO Constitution. The treaty officially came into effect on February 27, 2005. By this time, it had been signed by 168 countries and was legally binding in 154 of these nations that had ratified it, collectively representing a population of over 3 billion people. However, notable exceptions include Russia, which has not signed the treaty, and the United States, which has signed but not ratified it. The United States has attempted to modify certain provisions of the treaty but has achieved only limited success. For example, the treaty mandates that warning labels on tobacco products must be written in the language of the country where the products are sold. Additionally, the treaty prohibits the use of deceptive or misleading terms such as low tar or ultra-light in the marketing of tobacco products, even if such restrictions might conflict with trademark protections.
